bibliography.abstract: Preferences for travel-based activities may lead individuals to choose travel modes that best accommodate activity needs. In theory, “passengerised” modes, such as public transport and automated vehicles (AVs), could become the preferred travel options, as they enable a wider range of travel-based activities. This potential to use in-vehicle time could, in turn, decrease the value of travel time savings (VTTS), leading to lower resistance to longer journeys. Together, these two phenomena create challenges to demand modellers associated, including (i) mode choice self-selection associated with travel-based activities, and (ii) potential endogeneity bias in VTTS estimates. This study employs an attitude-based approach to capture mode choice self-selection while controlling for endogeneity bias in VTTS estimates by considering traveller characteristics and travel context variables that influence travel time use and account for value of time heterogeneity. Results suggest that the construct capturing the causal effect of travel time use on mode choice increases the probability of choosing rail modes in journeys over 5 km and car driving in journeys shorter than 5 km, confirming the presence of mode choice self-selection. Concerning VTTS, accounting for travel-time-use-related preferences and travel context characteristics led to travel-based activities having non-significant effects on VTTS, suggesting this approach may effectively control for endogeneity bias. These findings have implications for road safety, residential location choice, and potential AV-related behavioural changes, all of which have consequences for transport policy formulation. Overall, this study highlights the importance of accounting for travel time use to achieve a more realistic representation of activity-travel behaviour.

bibliography.title: Modelling the effects of travel time use on mode choice and the value of travel time savings: tackling self-selection and endogeneity bias

publication_status.journal: Transportation Research Part A Policy and Practice

en.caveats: The study relies on self-reported attitudes and preferences to capture travel time use, which may introduce measurement errors compared to direct observations of in-transit behavior.
en.what: This study models how travel-based activity preferences influence mode choice and the value of travel time savings (VTTS) using an attitude-based approach. The model controls for endogeneity and self-selection by incorporating traveller characteristics and travel context variables. The findings show that travel time use preferences increase the probability of choosing rail for trips longer than 5 km and car driving for trips under 5 km, while travel-based activities showed non-significant effects on VTTS once these preferences and context variables were controlled.
en.why: It demonstrates that accounting for travel-time-use preferences and context variables can effectively eliminate endogeneity bias in VTTS estimates, providing a more accurate framework for predicting mode shifts toward public transport or autonomous vehicles.
